analysis.one_liner: Caps private-insulin insurance copays at $35 a month.
analysis.headline: The bill won 102 Democratic cosponsors in the House but never received a committee vote or a floor vote before the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require private health plans to cover at least one insulin of each type and dose form, charge no deductible on it, and cap the patient's share of the cost at $35 a month or 25% of the negotiated price, whichever is lower. It applies to employer plans, individual market plans, and even bare-bones catastrophic plans. It does not change the underlying list price of insulin, only what patients pay out of pocket.
analysis.who_benefits: Millions of Americans who take insulin through private insurance. Anyone whose plan applied a deductible or high coinsurance to insulin would pay no more than $35 a month for a 30-day supply of the insulin products their plan selects. The cap counts toward deductibles and out-of-pocket maximums, so patients keep credit for what they do pay.

how_it_helps.text: Caps patient cost-sharing for a 30-day insulin supply at the lesser of $35 or 25% of the plan's negotiated price, starting in plan year 2024.

Bans applying a deductible to selected insulin products and requires plans to cover at least one product of each dosage form (vial, pump, inhaler) and each insulin type (rapid-, short-, intermediate-, long-, ultra long-acting, and premixed).
Requires catastrophic health plans — which normally pay nothing until a patient spends thousands out of pocket — to cover selected insulin products at the capped cost-sharing from day one.
Counts insulin cost-sharing toward deductibles and out-of-pocket maximums so patients still make progress toward their yearly caps.

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and the employers that sponsor group plans would absorb the cost of the cap, since the bill limits what patients pay without capping what plans pay manufacturers. To the extent plans can't fully negotiate the difference away, the cost could flow into premiums. Uninsured insulin users get nothing from this bill, and plans can still charge more than $35 at out-of-network pharmacies.

drawbacks.text: The bill caps only what patients pay, not the price of insulin itself; manufacturers keep their list prices, so the underlying cost problem stays in place and shifts to insurers and premiums.
Plans may charge more than $35 for insulin obtained from an out-of-network provider or pharmacy, so the cap is not airtight.
The cap does not apply to insulin products not selected by the plan, and people without insurance — a group disproportionately likely to ration insulin — are not covered at all.
A good-faith objection from plans and employers is that a federal cost-sharing floor mandate raises benefit costs, which show up as premiums or wages rather than disappearing.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For insulin users facing deductibles and coinsurance, a $35 monthly cap is a large, direct, and immediate benefit. The real weakness is that the bill leaves the high price of insulin untouched: it protects patients at the pharmacy counter while insurers and employers absorb the bill, and it leaves uninsured people out entirely. It is a genuine relief measure, not a price fix.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to three House committees and then to a Health Subcommittee, but no committee ever voted to advance it, and it died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Angie Craig introduced the bill on March 9, 2023, and it was referred to the Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, and Education and the Workforce Committees.

On March 17, 2023, it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Health Subcommittee, where it sat; it was referred to the same subcommittee again on December 17, 2024, with no markup or vote in between.
The bill ended the Congress with no committee vote, no floor vote, and no Senate companion action, the typical end for bills that stop in subcommittee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers and employers that sponsor group health plans are better off, because they never took on a federal mandate to cap insulin cost-sharing at $35 a month. Insulin manufacturers also keep their pricing structure intact, since the bill never touched list prices. Insulin users on private plans keep paying whatever their plan charges.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Insurers and employers; insulin users gained nothing

for.name: Rep. Angie Craig
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Affordable Insulin Now Act on March 9, 2023.

for.name: 102 of 216 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors of the bill.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.role: Primary committee of referral; chaired by Rep. Cathy McMorris Rodgers (R-WA) in this Congress
against.what_they_did: Held the bill in its Health Subcommittee for the entire Congress without a markup or vote to advance it.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee and House Education and the Workforce Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral; with three committees holding pieces of it, no panel ever moved it forward.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 102 cosponsors were Democrats; no House Republican signed on, and the Republican-run committees never advanced the bill.

industries.note: The bill would force insurers to cover selected insulin products with no deductible and at most $35 in patient cost-sharing per month, absorbing the difference themselves. Killing the bill avoided that mandate; the industry's gain here is exactly the cost insulin users would have been spared.

Because the bill amends ERISA, it applies directly to employer group health plans, which would bear the cost of the cap for their employees. The bill's death leaves employer plans free to keep applying deductibles to insulin.

The bill caps what patients pay but not the list or negotiated price of insulin, so manufacturers keep their pricing power while patient cost-sharing falls — and insulin stays inside private plans as the delivery channel. Insurers, in turn, may lean harder on manufacturers for price concessions to cover the cap.
